title: Bioluminescence: Living Lights
summary: How living things such as fireflies, deep-sea fish, squid, and plankton make their own cold light, and how they use it to send signals, catch prey, hide, and escape.
poll: Making light is one of the most useful skills an animal can have.

versions.title: Living Lights
versions.text:
Some things that live can glow. A bug can glow. A fish can glow. It is not a lamp. The light comes from the body. This has a long name. It is bioluminescence.

How does it work? Two things mix in the body. One is made in the body. The next is air. They mix and make light. The light is not hot. It is cool.

A firefly is a bug. It flies at night. It makes a flash. The flash is a signal. It helps the bugs find each other.

The deep sea is dark. Lots of sea life glows there. One fish has a light on its head. The light is a lure. Small fish swim up to it. Snap! The fish eats its prey.

Some sea life glows to hide. Some squirts a bright cloud. Then it swims off.

Tiny plankton glow too. Waves shake them. The sea shines blue.

In the Red Sea, a small fish has lights by its eyes.

People in labs use the glow too. It helps them see cells.

Some sea animals glow to hide. Others squirt a bright cloud. Then they swim away fast.

Tiny plankton glow too. When waves shake them, the sea shines blue.

In the Red Sea, a small fish has lights under its eyes.

Scientists use the glow, too. It helps them see cells.

versions.title: Bioluminescence: Living Lights
versions.text:
Some living things can make their own light. A firefly can glow. So can many fish in the sea. This light does not come from a lamp or the sun. It comes from inside the body. Scientists call it bioluminescence.

How does it work? Two things mix inside the animal. One is a special glow chemical made by the body. The other is oxygen. When they mix, they give off light. This light is cool, not hot.

A firefly is a beetle that flies at night. It flashes its light on and off. Each flash is a signal. Each kind of firefly has its own pattern. The flashes help fireflies find each other.

The deep sea is very dark. Many animals that live there can glow. The anglerfish has a light on a long rod above its mouth. The light is a lure. Small fish swim close to see it. Then the anglerfish gulps down its prey.

Some sea animals glow to hide from danger. Some squid and shrimp squirt out a bright cloud. While the enemy looks at the cloud, they swim away.

Tiny living things called plankton glow too. When waves shake them, the water shines blue.

In the Red Sea, the flashlight fish has lights under its eyes.

Scientists use the glow as well. It helps them see tiny cells.

versions.title: Bioluminescence: Living Lights
versions.text:
On a dark night, a small light blinks in the grass. Far below the ocean waves, a fish shines like a lantern. Both of these lights come from living things. Scientists call this bioluminescence, which means "living light."

The light is made inside the body. A special glow chemical mixes with oxygen, and the mix gives off light. Unlike a light bulb, this light makes almost no heat. That is why people call it cold light.

Fireflies are beetles that use their light to talk. They flash in a pattern, and each flash is a signal. Every kind of firefly has its own pattern. This helps fireflies find each other in the dark.

The deep sea gets no sunlight at all. Many of the animals that live there can glow. The anglerfish has a glowing tip on a rod above its mouth. This light is a lure. When a small fish swims close to look, the anglerfish snaps up its prey.

Light can also help animals hide. Some fish have a soft glow on their bellies. From below, they blend in with the faint light from above. Some squid and shrimp squirt a glowing cloud at an enemy and then escape.

Tiny plankton glow when waves shake them, so the water sparkles blue at night.

The Red Sea is home to the flashlight fish. It has glowing spots under its eyes.

Today, scientists borrow glowing chemicals to help them see tiny cells.

versions.title: Bioluminescence: Nature's Living Lights
versions.text:
On a summer night, tiny lights blink above a field. Deep in the ocean, a fish shines like a small lantern. Neither light comes from a battery or the sun. Both are made by living things. Scientists call this bioluminescence, which means "living light."

The light comes from a chemical reaction inside the body. A special glow chemical joins with oxygen, and the reaction gives off energy as light. Unlike a light bulb, it makes almost no heat, so it is often called cold light.

Fireflies are beetles that flash their light to talk to each other. Each flash is a signal, and every kind of firefly has its own pattern of blinks. The patterns help fireflies attract and find one another.

The deep sea gets no sunlight, yet many animals that live there can glow. The anglerfish has a glowing tip on a rod that hangs over its mouth. Small fish are attracted to the light. They swim closer and become prey.

Light can also be a kind of camouflage. Some fish and squid glow softly on their bellies. When a predator looks up from below, the glow blends with the dim light from above, so the animal is hard to see. Other squid and shrimp squirt a glowing cloud at a predator and escape while it is confused.

Tiny plankton glow when waves shake them, so the sea sparkles blue at night. Most sea light is blue because blue light travels farthest through water.

In the Red Sea, the flashlight fish has glowing spots under its eyes. Scientists have even borrowed glowing chemicals to light up cells so they can study them.

versions.title: Bioluminescence: Nature's Living Lights
versions.text:
On a warm night, tiny lights may blink above a field. Deep in the ocean, a fish may shine like a lantern in total darkness. Neither of these lights comes from a battery, a fire, or the sun. Both are made by living things, and scientists call this skill bioluminescence, which means "living light."

The light is the result of a chemical reaction. Inside special cells, a glowing chemical joins with oxygen, and the reaction lets out energy in the form of light. Unlike a normal light bulb, it makes almost no heat, which is why it is often called cold light.

Fireflies, which are really beetles, flash their light to send messages. Each flash is a signal, and every kind of firefly has its own pattern of blinks. These patterns help fireflies attract and find one another in the dark.

Sunlight never reaches the deep sea, yet a large number of the animals that live there can glow. The anglerfish dangles a glowing tip on a rod above its mouth. Small fish are attracted to the light, swim closer to take a look, and quickly become prey.

Light can also work as camouflage. Some fish and squid glow faintly on their bellies. When a predator looks up from below, the glow matches the dim light coming down from the surface, so the animal almost disappears. Other squid and shrimp let out a glowing cloud to confuse a predator while they swim away.

Tiny plankton glow when waves shake them, which makes the water sparkle blue at night. Most light in the ocean is blue because blue light travels farthest through water.

In the Red Sea, the flashlight fish has glowing spots beneath its eyes. Scientists have even borrowed glowing chemicals from nature to light up cells so they can study them.

versions.title: Bioluminescence: Nature's Living Lights
versions.text:
On a warm evening, tiny lights may flicker above a field, while far below the ocean waves a fish may shine like a lantern in total darkness. Neither light comes from a battery, a flame, or the sun. Both are produced by living things, and scientists call this amazing ability bioluminescence, which means "living light."

The glow is the result of a chemical reaction. Inside special cells, a light-making chemical combines with oxygen, and the reaction releases energy as light instead of heat. Because almost no warmth is produced, scientists often describe bioluminescence as cold light.

Fireflies, which are actually beetles, flash their lights to send messages. Each flash is a signal, and every kind of firefly has its own pattern of blinks, so fireflies can attract and recognize members of their own kind.

Sunlight never reaches the deep ocean, yet a large share of the creatures that live there can glow. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure from a rod above its huge mouth. Curious small fish are attracted to the light, swim closer to look, and quickly become prey.

Light can also serve as camouflage. Some fish and squid glow faintly along their bellies, so when a predator looks up from below, the glow matches the dim light coming down from the surface and the animal almost disappears. Other squid and shrimp release a glowing cloud that confuses a predator while they escape.

Tiny plankton glow when waves disturb them, which makes some beaches sparkle blue at night. Most ocean light is blue because blue light travels farthest through water.

Living light is not only found in the sea. Some mushrooms glow a soft green in damp forests, and scientists think the glow may draw insects that carry their spores to new places.

In the Red Sea, the flashlight fish carries glowing patches beneath its eyes. Scientists have even borrowed glowing chemicals from nature to light up cells so that they can study them.

versions.title: Bioluminescence: The Chemistry of Living Light
versions.text:
On a warm evening, tiny lights may flicker above a meadow, while hundreds of meters beneath the ocean surface a fish may shine like a lantern in complete darkness. Neither light comes from a battery, a flame, or the sun; both are produced by living organisms, and scientists call this remarkable ability bioluminescence, which means "living light."

The glow results from a chemical reaction. Inside special cells, a molecule called luciferin combines with oxygen, and an enzyme called luciferase speeds up the reaction, which releases energy as visible light rather than heat. Because almost no warmth is produced, scientists often describe bioluminescence as cold light.

Fireflies, which are actually beetles, flash their lights to communicate, and every species has its own pattern of blinks so that fireflies can recognize members of their own kind in the dark.

Sunlight never reaches the deep ocean, yet a large share of the creatures that live there can glow. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure from a bendy rod above its enormous mouth, and curious smaller fish that swim close to investigate quickly become prey.

Light can also provide camouflage through a strategy called counterillumination. Certain fish and squid glow faintly along their undersides, so that when a predator looks upward, the glow matches the dim light filtering down from the surface and the animal practically vanishes. Other squid and shrimp release a glowing cloud that distracts a predator while they escape.

Tiny plankton glow whenever waves disturb them, which causes some shorelines to sparkle at night. Most light in the sea is blue-green because that wavelength travels farthest through seawater.

Living light is not found only in the ocean. Some mushrooms glow a soft green in damp forests, and scientists think that the glow may attract insects, which then carry the mushroom's spores to new places.

In the Red Sea, the flashlight fish carries glowing patches beneath its eyes, and those patches are full of symbiotic bacteria that make the light in exchange for food and a safe home. Researchers have also borrowed a glowing protein from a jellyfish to light up living cells, an idea that later earned a Nobel Prize.

versions.title: Bioluminescence: The Chemistry of Living Light
versions.text:
On a warm, tranquil evening, tiny lights may flicker intermittently above an open meadow, while simultaneously, hundreds of meters beneath the ocean's surface, a solitary fish may shine persistently like a lantern suspended within complete, impenetrable darkness. Neither source of light originates from a battery, an open flame, or the distant sun, since both are instead produced entirely by living organisms themselves, and scientists consequently refer to this remarkable biological capability as bioluminescence, a term signifying "living light."

This characteristic glow results specifically from a chemical reaction in which a molecule called luciferin combines directly with oxygen within specialized cells, while an accompanying enzyme called luciferase simultaneously accelerates the entire process, ensuring that the resulting released energy emerges predominantly as visible light rather than as dissipated heat. Because almost no appreciable warmth is generated through this process, scientists frequently and appropriately describe bioluminescence as cold light, considerably more energy-efficient than any conventional artificial bulb.

Fireflies, which constitute a type of beetle rather than a true fly, flash their characteristic lights specifically to communicate with potential mates, and each distinct species produces its own unique pattern of rhythmic blinks, enabling individual fireflies to recognize members of their own particular species amid the surrounding darkness.

Although direct sunlight never manages to penetrate the deep ocean's crushing depths, a considerable proportion of the creatures inhabiting this lightless realm are nevertheless able to generate their own glow. The anglerfish dangles a luminous lure suspended from a flexible appendage positioned above its enormous, cavernous mouth, and curious smaller fish that approach to investigate this tempting light quickly become its unsuspecting prey.

Living light can also provide effective camouflage through a specialized strategy known as counterillumination: certain fish and squid species glow faintly along their undersides, so that when a predator subsequently gazes upward from below, this carefully matched glow corresponds precisely with the dim ambient light filtering downward from the distant surface, and the vulnerable animal consequently becomes practically invisible against this backdrop. Other squid and shrimp species instead release an entire luminous cloud that effectively distracts an approaching attacker while they themselves make a hasty escape.

Microscopic plankton organisms glow conspicuously whenever passing waves physically disturb them, a phenomenon causing entire coastal shorelines to sparkle dramatically at night, and the majority of light generated within the sea appears distinctly blue-green specifically because that particular wavelength travels considerably farther through seawater than other colors.

Living light is certainly not confined exclusively to the ocean environment, since certain mushroom species glow with a soft greenish hue within damp forest environments, and scientists suspect that this subtle glow may function to attract insects, which subsequently carry the mushroom's reproductive spores toward entirely new locations where they can successfully germinate and grow.

In the Red Sea specifically, the flashlight fish carries distinctive glowing patches positioned directly beneath its eyes, and these specialized patches are densely packed with symbiotic bacteria that collaboratively produce the visible light in direct exchange for essential nutrients and physical shelter. Researchers have additionally borrowed a fluorescent protein originally derived from jellyfish specifically to illuminate living cells for scientific study, a valuable technique considered so significant for medical research that its original discoverers subsequently received a prestigious Nobel Prize.

versions.text:

This characteristic glow results specifically from a sophisticated chemical reaction in which a molecule called luciferin combines directly with available oxygen within specialized cells, while an accompanying enzyme called luciferase simultaneously accelerates this entire biochemical process, thereby ensuring that the resulting released energy emerges predominantly as visible light rather than as wastefully dissipated heat. Because almost no appreciable warmth is generated through this remarkably efficient process, scientists frequently and quite appropriately describe bioluminescence as cold light, considerably more energy-efficient in its operation than any conventional artificial bulb ever manufactured.

Fireflies, which constitute a particular type of beetle rather than a true fly in the technical biological sense, flash their characteristic lights specifically to communicate with potential mates across considerable distances, and each distinct species produces its own entirely unique pattern of rhythmic blinks, thereby enabling individual fireflies to recognize members of their own particular species amid the surrounding, enveloping darkness.

Although direct sunlight never manages to penetrate the deep ocean's crushing, lightless depths, a considerable proportion of the diverse creatures inhabiting this permanently lightless realm are nevertheless able to generate their own self-produced glow. The anglerfish dangles a luminous lure suspended from a flexible appendage positioned directly above its enormous, cavernous mouth, and curious smaller fish that approach cautiously to investigate this tempting light quickly become its unsuspecting prey.

Living light can also provide remarkably effective camouflage through a specialized evolutionary strategy known as counterillumination: certain fish and squid species glow faintly along their undersides, so that when a predator subsequently gazes upward from beneath, this carefully matched glow corresponds precisely with the dim ambient light filtering downward from the distant surface above, and the vulnerable animal consequently becomes practically invisible against this uniform backdrop. Other squid and shrimp species instead release an entire luminous cloud into the water that effectively distracts an approaching attacker while they themselves make a hasty, strategic escape.

Microscopic plankton organisms glow conspicuously and dramatically whenever passing waves physically disturb their delicate bodies, a striking phenomenon causing entire coastal shorelines to sparkle dramatically at night, and the overwhelming majority of light generated within the sea appears distinctly blue-green specifically because that particular wavelength travels considerably farther through seawater than any competing color in the visible spectrum.

Living light is certainly not confined exclusively to the ocean environment, since certain mushroom species glow with a soft, almost ethereal greenish hue within damp forest environments, and scientists strongly suspect that this subtle glow may function specifically to attract passing insects, which subsequently carry the mushroom's reproductive spores toward entirely new locations where they can successfully germinate and continue growing.

Researchers have additionally borrowed a naturally fluorescent protein originally derived from jellyfish specifically to illuminate living cells for detailed scientific study, a valuable laboratory technique considered so significant for medical research that its original discoverers subsequently received a prestigious Nobel Prize in recognition of its importance.

wrong.B: The light makes almost no heat, and salt is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Plankton make light themselves; they are not one of the two chemicals.

questions.stem: Why is bioluminescence called cold light?
options: It only happens in cold water.
It makes almost no heat.
It is always blue.
It only shines in winter.
questions.why: The article says that, unlike a light bulb, living light makes almost no heat.

wrong.A: Fireflies glow on warm nights, so it is not only in cold water.
wrong.C: Being blue is about how light travels in water, not why it is called cold.
wrong.D: The article says nothing about winter.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: "Light can also be a kind of camouflage." What does camouflage mean here?
options: A way to look brighter than everything else
A way to call other animals
A way to blend in so you are hard to see
A way to make food
questions.why: The belly glow blends with the light from above so the animal is hard to see, which is camouflage.

wrong.A: Camouflage hides an animal; it does not make it stand out.
wrong.B: Calling other animals is what firefly signals do.
wrong.D: Camouflage has nothing to do with making food.

questions.stem: A fish glows softly on its belly. Why would a predator swimming below it have trouble seeing it?
options: The glow blinds the predator.
The glow matches the dim light coming from above.
The glow makes the fish look bigger.
The predator is afraid of light.
questions.why: The article says the belly glow blends with the dim light from the surface, so the fish almost disappears.

wrong.A: The glow is soft and faint, not blinding.
wrong.C: The article does not say the glow changes the fish's size.
wrong.D: Predators like the anglerfish's prey swim toward light, so fear is not the reason.

questions.stem: Why is most of the light made by sea animals blue?
options: Blue light travels farthest through water.
Blue is the only color animals can see.
Sea water turns all light blue.
Blue light is the warmest color.
questions.why: The article says blue light travels farthest through water, so blue light is the most useful underwater.

wrong.B: The article never says animals can see only blue.
wrong.C: The article gives a different reason: blue travels farthest.
wrong.D: Living light makes almost no heat, so warmth is not the reason.

questions.stem: Each kind of firefly has its own pattern of blinks. What can you infer from this?
options: Fireflies blink at random with no purpose.
All fireflies are the same kind.
Fireflies blink to warm their wings.
A firefly can tell which flashes come from its own kind.
questions.why: Different patterns let fireflies recognize and attract members of their own kind.

wrong.A: The article says the flashes are signals with a purpose.
wrong.B: The article says there are different kinds with different patterns.
wrong.C: The light is cold, so it does not warm anything.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the middle of the article?
options: By telling events in the order they happened in history
By describing different ways animals use their light
By comparing living light to fire step by step
By listing rules for visiting the sea
questions.why: The middle paragraphs each show a use of light: sending signals, catching prey, hiding, and escaping.

wrong.A: The article is not a history told in time order.
wrong.C: Fire is mentioned only once; it is not the structure.
wrong.D: There are no rules for visiting the sea.

MID.prompt: Explain how bioluminescence helps animals in the deep sea survive. Use at least two examples from the article.
checklist: I gave at least two examples of animals from the article.
I explained how the light helps each animal survive.
MID.modelAnswer: Bioluminescence is light made by a living thing, and in the deep sea, animals use it in clever ways to survive. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure that can attract small fish close enough to catch and eat, turning its own body into a trap for its prey. Other fish and squid use their glow as camouflage, letting their bellies match the faint light coming from above so a predator looking up from below cannot easily see them. In both cases, this living light gives deep-sea animals a real advantage in a place where sunlight never reaches.

keyWords.definition: a chemical in some living things that gives off light when it joins with oxygen
keyWords.example: Scientists added luciferin to the test tube and watched it begin to shine.

keyWords.definition: a substance made by living things that speeds up a chemical change
keyWords.example: An enzyme in your saliva starts breaking down bread while you chew.

keyWords.definition: a way of hiding by glowing to match the light behind you
keyWords.example: Thanks to counterillumination, the shrimp was almost invisible from below.

keyWords.definition: the size of a light or sound wave, which decides its color or pitch
keyWords.example: Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light.

keyWords.definition: living closely together in a way that helps both living things
keyWords.example: The clownfish and the sea anemone have a symbiotic relationship.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Bioluminescence is a rare accident of nature that does not help living things in any real way.
Only ocean animals are able to produce light.
Living light is made by a chemical reaction and serves many purposes for survival.
Bioluminescence was first discovered in a laboratory.
questions.why: The article explains the chemistry of living light and then shows how it is used to communicate, hunt, hide, escape, and even spread spores.

wrong.A: Every example in the article shows the light has a purpose.
wrong.B: Fireflies and mushrooms glow on land.
wrong.D: The article describes light found in nature; scientists borrowed it later.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is the job of luciferase?
options: It speeds up the reaction between luciferin and oxygen.
It collects sunlight during the day and stores it so the animal can shine later at night.
It turns the light from blue to red.
It is the bacteria that live in the flashlight fish.
questions.why: The article calls luciferase an enzyme that speeds up (accelerates) the reaction that releases light.

wrong.B: Living light does not come from stored sunlight.
wrong.C: The article does not say luciferase changes colors.
wrong.D: The flashlight fish's light comes from bacteria; luciferase is an enzyme.

questions.stem: How does the flashlight fish of the Red Sea get its light?
options: It reflects moonlight with its scales.
Symbiotic bacteria in patches under its eyes make the light.
It swallows large amounts of glowing plankton every night, and their light shows through its skin.
It borrows a protein from jellyfish.
questions.why: The article says patches under its eyes are packed with symbiotic bacteria that produce the light in exchange for food and shelter.

wrong.A: The article does not mention reflected moonlight.
wrong.C: Eating plankton is not given as the source of its light.
wrong.D: Scientists, not the fish, borrowed a jellyfish protein.

questions.stem: In the article, the bacteria and the flashlight fish are described as symbiotic. Which detail best shows this meaning?
options: The fish lives in the Red Sea.
The patches are beneath the fish's eyes.
The bacteria make light while the fish gives them food and shelter.
The light it gives off is blue-green, the color that travels farthest through seawater.
questions.why: Symbiotic means both partners benefit, and the exchange of light for food and shelter shows that.

wrong.A: Where the fish lives does not show a helping relationship.
wrong.B: The location of the patches does not explain the partnership.
wrong.D: The color of light is not about two living things helping each other.

questions.stem: Why would counterillumination fail to protect a fish if its belly glowed much more brightly than the light coming from the surface?
options: Because the brighter glow would make the fish stand out against the dim background
Because bright light uses up all the oxygen in the sea
Because predators can only see red light
Because the fish would become too warm
questions.why: Counterillumination works by matching the dim light above; a glow that is too bright would not match and would reveal the fish.

wrong.B: The article does not say glowing uses up the ocean's oxygen.
wrong.C: The article says most sea light is blue-green, not that predators see only red.
wrong.D: Bioluminescence is cold light, so heat is not the problem.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why deep-sea animals mostly glow blue-green instead of red?
options: Red light is too hot for the deep sea.
Their predators prefer red.
Blue-green light would be seen over a greater distance underwater.
Red chemicals cannot mix with oxygen.
questions.why: The article says blue-green is the wavelength that travels farthest through seawater, so it is the most visible color there.

wrong.A: Living light is cold, so heat is not the issue.
wrong.B: Nothing in the article says predators prefer red.
wrong.D: The article does not discuss red chemicals.

questions.stem: How does the anglerfish's use of light differ from the squid's glowing cloud?
options: The anglerfish uses light to escape, while the squid uses it to hunt.
Both use light only to talk with members of their own kind.
The anglerfish uses light to attract prey, while the squid uses it to distract an attacker.
Both use light to warm the water around them.
questions.why: The anglerfish's lure draws smaller fish in to eat, while the squid's cloud distracts a predator so it can escape.

wrong.B: Communication is how fireflies use light, not these sea animals.
wrong.D: Living light produces almost no heat.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the jellyfish protein and the Nobel Prize at the end?
options: To argue that jellyfish are the most important sea animals
To show that studying living light has also been valuable to people
To explain how fireflies choose their blinking patterns
To warn readers that glowing animals are dangerous
questions.why: The ending shows that scientists use glowing proteins to study cells, a discovery valuable enough to win a major prize.

wrong.A: The article does not rank sea animals by importance.
wrong.C: Firefly patterns are discussed earlier and have nothing to do with the prize.
wrong.D: The article never says glowing animals are dangerous to people.

HIGH.prompt: Bioluminescence can help an animal be seen or help it stay hidden. Explain how both can be true, using at least two examples from the article.
checklist: I explained how light can help an animal be seen.
I explained how light can help an animal stay hidden.
I supported my explanation with at least two examples from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Bioluminescence can help an animal be seen when it needs to attract something, as when the anglerfish dangles a glowing lure that pulls curious prey within striking distance. Fireflies rely on the same visibility, flashing distinct patterns of light so other fireflies of the same kind can find them in the dark. At the same time, bioluminescence can help an animal disappear through counterillumination, where a fish or squid glows faintly on its belly to match the wavelength of dim light filtering down from the surface, so a predator looking upward sees no shadow at all. Because the same chemical glow can either call attention to an animal or erase its outline completely, bioluminescence proves to be a remarkably flexible survival tool in the deep sea.
